approved: Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2019
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would merge the Federal Circuit Court and the Family Court into a single court called the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia.
The new court would have two divisions, with one Chief Justice and a unified case management system to handle family law matters more efficiently.
The bill would not allow decided family law cases to be reopened just because of these changes.
Creates the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia as an overarching structure.
Establishes two divisions: Division 1 continues the Family Court, and Division 2 continues the Federal Circuit Court.
Provides for a single point of entry for family law matters, filed in Division 2 and transferred to Division 1 as needed.
Places the court under the leadership of one Chief Justice and one Deputy Chief Justice with dual commissions.
Preserves the Federal Circuit Court's general federal law and fair work jurisdiction in Division 2.
Allows the Chief Justice and Chief Judge to make Rules of Court alone for the first two years.
Australian families involved in family law disputes and the federal family court system.

Moved the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill, which merges the Family Court and Federal Circuit Court into a single administrative structure with one point of entry, and announced an extra $4 million to help courts implement the reforms and $3.7 million for an additional judge.

The bill facilitates the transition from the Family Court and Federal Circuit Court to the new Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (FCFC), repealing and amending parts of the Family Law Act 1975 and the Federal Circuit Court Act 1999, and includes transitional arrangements for pending matters. It addresses five recommendations from the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee's February 2019 report.

The speaker argued that merging the Family Court of Australia into the Federal Circuit Court would harm vulnerable families by undermining specialist family law expertise, and criticised the government's lack of consultation and evidence. The speaker called for the bills to be withdrawn and for increased resources and adoption of the Australian Law Reform Commission's 2019 recommendations.

The speaker argued that the family law system is broken and that the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2019 will improve it by creating a unified court structure with a single point of entry, reducing costs and delays. They cited consistent evidence from inquiries of a broken system, noted that 88% of family law cases are handled by the Federal Circuit Court, and detailed $87.3 million in funding for family law services and the Lighthouse Project pilot for family safety screening.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2019, arguing it would abolish the specialist Family Court, worsen delays averaging 18.6 months in the Family Court and 17.5 months in the Federal Circuit Court, and ignore expert recommendations. They criticised the government for neglecting the family law system under Prime Ministers Abbott, Turnbull, and Morrison, and supported an amendment by the shadow Attorney-General.

The speaker argued that the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2019 would abolish the specialised Family Court, putting vulnerable children and families at risk, and noted that over 110 stakeholders, including the Peninsula Community Legal Centre and the Law Council of Australia, oppose the merger. The speaker cited concerns from former Chief Justices Elizabeth Evatt and Alastair Nicholson, and stated the bill would not increase efficiency or save money, but could cost lives.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2019, arguing it would abolish the specialised Family Court and merge it with the already overburdened Federal Circuit Court, harming vulnerable families and children. She noted that over 110 stakeholders oppose the merger, and the bill fails to address resourcing issues, judge workloads, or family violence risks.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2019, arguing it would gradually abolish the specialist Family Court and worsen outcomes for families, and criticised the government for ignoring 33 recommendations from a parliamentary inquiry and failing to consult stakeholders.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2019 and related bills, arguing they would abolish the specialist Family Court and merge it into an overstretched generalist Federal Circuit Court. The speaker noted that no recommendation for such a merger came from the Australian Law Reform Commission review, the Joint Select Committee on Australia's Family Law System, or any of 67 previous inquiries, and cited opposition from former Chief Justices Elizabeth Evatt and Alastair Nicholson, the Law Council of Australia, and other legal bodies.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill merger, arguing it lacks additional resources, will not reduce delays or backlogs, and is opposed by over 110 stakeholders including the Law Council and former Family Court justices. The speaker also noted the merger is based on a flawed six-week PwC review and that the government has not responded to the Australian Law Reform Commission's 60 recommendations for family law reform.

The speaker argued against the government's proposed merger of the Family Court and Federal Circuit Court, calling instead for a standalone specialist Family Court with a "Family Court 2.0" model, and opposed the bill as based on a six-week desktop review rather than evidence. The speaker also called for at least $310 million per year in additional funding for legal assistance providers and adequate resourcing of the courts.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2019, arguing it would abolish the specialist Family Court and harm vulnerable families and children, citing average caseloads of 337 per Federal Circuit Court judge, trial delays of 18.6 months in the Family Court and 17.5 months in the Federal Circuit Court, and up to 12 months for family reports. They noted that 110 stakeholders, including the Law Council of Australia and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Legal Services, opposed the merger, and that the government relied on a discredited PricewaterhouseCoopers desktop review rather than independent reports.

Labor opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2019, arguing it abolishes the specialist Family Court, harms vulnerable women and children, and follows years of government neglect; the speaker cited over 110 organisations' opposition and supported the shadow attorney-general's amendment to reject the legislation.

The speaker argued that the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2019 and related bill will dismantle the Family Court system, adversely affecting families and children, and criticized the coalition for underfunding, failing to appoint enough judges, and ignoring opposition from 110 individuals and organisations.

Labor opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2019, arguing the merger would harm vulnerable families and children by diluting specialist expertise. The party called for proper resourcing and judicial appointments instead, citing the Australian Law Reform Commission's 60 recommendations and widespread expert opposition.

The government's bill to abolish the Family Court is a radical, unjustified change that ignores expert opposition from former chief justices, the Law Council and the Australian Law Reform Commission, and is based on under-resourcing rather than structural problems.

The speaker called for addressing court underfunding and under-resourcing instead of merging the courts.
